topic: Dimensional Portals: Geometrically Visualizing Non-Square Matrices
target_audience: University students or advanced high school students learning Linear Algebra

outline.topic: Dimensional Portals: Geometrically Visualizing Non-Square Matrices
outline.target_audience: University students or advanced high school students learning Linear Algebra

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Matrix as a Map Maker
sections.content: Briefly review that a matrix transformation is defined by where it moves the basis vectors (i-hat and j-hat). In a square 2x2 matrix, we move from a 2D plane to a 2D plane. Establish the 'Grid-to-Grid' visual.
sections.example: Visualize a standard 2D grid. If a matrix is [[2, 1], [0, 1]], the grid squares turn into parallelograms, but the world stays flat.

sections.title: Tall Matrices: Moving from 2D to 3D
sections.content: Introduce a 3x2 matrix. Explain that it takes a 2-coordinate input and outputs a 3-coordinate vector. Geometrically, this means mapping a 2D 'sheet' into 3D space. The two basis vectors of the 2D plane land somewhere in 3D space, defining a tilted plane passing through the origin.
sections.example: A 2D 'Flatland' character walks onto a 3x2 matrix portal. He is still 'flat' but is now floating like a piece of paper tilted in a 3D room. His new coordinates are (x, y, z), but he can only reach points on that specific 2D slice of the 3D world.

sections.title: Wide Matrices: The Great Squish (3D to 2D)
sections.content: Introduce a 2x3 matrix. This takes a 3D vector and outputs a 2D vector. Explain that the three basis vectors of 3D space (i, j, k) are 'squashed' onto a 2D plane. This represents a loss of information, similar to a projection.
sections.example: Think of 'Shadow Puppetry.' A 3D bird (input) flies in front of a light. The 2x3 matrix is the light source that projects its 3D position onto a 2D wall (output). You can see where it is on the wall, but you lose the depth information.

sections.title: The Rule of Rows and Columns
sections.content: Synthesize the visual logic: The number of columns tells us the 'Input Dimensions' (how many basis vectors we are moving). The number of rows tells us the 'Output Dimensions' (how many coordinates each basis vector ends up having).
sections.example: A 100x2 matrix would take a simple 2D drawing and 'embed' it into a 100-dimensional hyper-space. It’s still just a 2D shape, but described with 100 coordinates.

sections.title: Summary: Linear Transformations as Dimensional Portals
sections.content: Conclude by emphasizing that non-square matrices are not just 'broken' square matrices; they are portals that allow us to move data between different levels of reality (dimensions). Reinforce the 'Column Space' concept visually.
sections.example: An animation showing a 2D circle being stretched into a 3D tube (Tall Matrix) and then flattened into a 1D line (Wide Matrix), illustrating the fluid transition between dimensions.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Matrix as a Map Maker
lecture_lines: Matrix transformations move the basis vectors i and j.
These vectors define how the entire grid transforms.
In square matrices, the plane remains two-dimensional.
animations: Draw a standard 2D grid (#555555) with basis vectors i-hat (#FF0000) and j-hat (#00FF00).
Display the matrix [[2, 1], [0, 1]] (#FFFFFF) in the top-right corner.
Animate the grid shearing so i-hat stays on x-axis (scaled) and j-hat tilts, forming parallelograms.

storyboard.title: Tall Matrices: Moving from 2D to 3D
lecture_lines: A three-by-two matrix maps two dimensions into three.
Two input basis vectors land in three-dimensional space.
This creates a tilted plane within the 3D world.
The input is flat, but the output has depth.
We call this embedding a lower dimension into higher.
animations: Display a 3x2 matrix (#FFFFFF) and 2D unit vectors (#FF0000, #00FF00) on a 2D plane.
Rotate the camera to a 3D perspective to reveal a z-axis (#888888).
Transform the 2D vectors into 3D vectors: [1, 0, 1] and [0, 1, 1].
Animate a faint 2D plane (#0000FF, 0.4 opacity) spanning the two 3D vectors.
Place a 2D character silhouette on the original plane and move it onto the tilted 3D plane.

storyboard.title: Wide Matrices: The Great Squish (3D to 2D)
lecture_lines: A two-by-three matrix squashes three dimensions into two.
Three basis vectors are flattened onto a flat plane.
Like shadow puppetry, we lose the dimension of depth.
Information is lost when projecting into fewer dimensions.
This transformation reduces the volume into an area.
animations: Display a 2x3 matrix (#FFFFFF) and three basis vectors in 3D space: i, j, k.
Flatten the 3D space onto a 2D plane, showing i, j, k as 2D vectors.
Show a 3D object (a cube wireframe) being projected into a 2D shadow (#FFFF00).
Highlight that the z-information is gone by showing different z-heights mapping to one 2D point.
Label the resulting 2D space as the "Output Space" (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: The Rule of Rows and Columns
lecture_lines: Columns represent the number of input basis vectors.
Rows represent the coordinates in the output space.
This simple rule governs all dimensional transformations.
animations: Display a large matrix with labels: 'Rows' (#FF0000) and 'Columns' (#00FF00).
Animate the 'Columns' label pointing to the 2D input space (2 vectors).
Animate the 'Rows' label pointing to the 3 coordinates of the output vectors.
Show a 100x2 matrix label and visualize a 2D grid 'embedding' into a dense set of lines (100D).
Highlight the text: 'Columns = Input Dim, Rows = Output Dim' (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Summary: Linear Transformations as Dimensional Portals
lecture_lines: Non-square matrices act as portals between different dimensions.
They map data across varying levels of reality.
Visualizing these shifts reveals the power of linear algebra.
animations: Show a 2D shape (#FFFFFF) transitioning into a 3D surface (#00FF00) via a tall matrix.
Squash that 3D surface into a 1D line segment (#FF0000) via a wide matrix.
Display the concluding text 'Linear Transformations: Dimensional Portals' (#FFFFFF).
